Follow the universal overnight-session-base workflow PLUS the

Read and follow overnight-session-base.md first, then apply these:

---

## NPC GAME-SPECIFIC: SPECIALIST AGENTS

| Issue type | Primary agent | Secondary agent |
|------------|--------------|-----------------|
| New NPC character | npc-dialogue-designer | game-state-auditor |
| New dialogue scenario | npc-dialogue-designer | — |
| New proposed action type | npc-dialogue-designer | game-state-auditor |
| Action validation / trust boundary | game-state-auditor | — |
| System prompt optimization | prompt-optimizer | — |
| Schema change | npc-dialogue-designer | game-state-auditor |
| C++ game engine change | (main agent with C++17 conventions) | game-state-auditor |

For ANY issue that introduces a new proposed_action type or modifies
the trust boundary, ALWAYS run game-state-auditor before committing.
This is non-negotiable — state corruption bugs are the worst failure mode.

---

## NPC GAME-SPECIFIC: CORE ARCHITECTURE (know this before touching anything)

Schema-as-contract: the LLM generates structured JSON. C++ renders it.
Never have the LLM generate code, assets, or UI layout.

Every NPC response must match this schema exactly:
```json
{
  "dialogue": "string",
  "mood": "curious|friendly|suspicious|hostile|neutral|afraid|happy|sad",
  "gesture": "nod|shake_head|point|shrug|wave|cross_arms|none",
  "internal_thought": "string (debug only, never shown to player)",
  "proposed_action": null,
  "relationship_delta": 0
}
```

proposed_action, when non-null:
```json
{
  "type": "give_item|start_quest|open_shop|share_information|refuse_service",
  "parameters": {},
  "trust_required": 0
}
```

The C++ validation layer decides whether to execute proposed_action.
The LLM NEVER executes actions directly. Ever.

---

## NPC GAME-SPECIFIC: TEST COMMANDS

```bash
# C++ build and test
mkdir -p build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
make -j4
ctest --output-on-failure
cd ..

# Schema validation — run after any NPC or schema change
python3 tests/validate_schema.py

# Dialogue smoke tests — 5 representative conversations per new NPC
python3 tests/test_npc_dialogue.py --npc [npc_name]
```

For new NPC characters, the smoke test is critical. Run:
- Normal conversation (on-topic)
- Off-topic question (should deflect)
- Player hostility (mood should shift)
- Low-trust proposed action (should be rejected by validation layer)

All outputs must be valid JSON matching the schema above.

---

## NPC GAME-SPECIFIC: HARD RULES

1. LLM output is untrusted input. Validate everything before executing.
2. Every new proposed_action type must be in the C++ validation allowlist.
   Adding a type to the schema without adding it to the allowlist is a bug.
3. trust_required in the JSON is NEVER trusted. The C++ layer uses the
   game state's trust score, not the value the LLM returns.
4. System prompts must be model-agnostic — must work on Ollama/Gemma,
   not only on expensive cloud models.
5. Token efficiency: no NPC system prompt should exceed 800 tokens.
   If it does, run prompt-optimizer before committing.
6. New NPC characters must have a knowledge domain and knowledge exclusions
   documented in the system prompt.
7. Conversation history is capped per NPC type — respect the cap.
   Do not add history injection that grows without bound.

---

For new NPC characters:
- Concept = the dialogue design pattern or NPC architecture
- "LLM NPC character constraint and knowledge domain design" ✅
- "Added the blacksmith NPC" ❌

# Plan: Weapons, HUD, Combat & LLM Reactions
Date: 2026-06-28
Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
Estimated complexity: XL

## The Idea (one paragraph)
Add a full combat layer to `cpp_game_with_llm_npcs`. The player gets health and an inventory of weapons (fists, pistol, at minimum); a HUD shows health, current weapon, and ammo. Attacking a civilian makes them take damage and flee. Cops are armed, fight back with probabilistic accuracy, and can take damage too. When an NPC is attacked or witnesses violence nearby, the game injects a combat-context message into their LLM prompt so they react in-character ("Hey! Hands where I can see them!") before switching to code-driven fight/flee AI.

## Goal
A player can pick a fight in the city, see visual feedback (HUD, animated attacks, a visible weapon in hand), watch NPCs flee or fight back, and have cops verbally challenge them via LLM before opening fire.

## Out of Scope (this version)
- Inventory UI / item pickup from the ground
- Multiple gun types beyond fist + pistol (no shotgun, rifle, etc.)
- NPC pathfinding beyond simple flee-away-from-player movement
- Multiplayer
- Persistent wanted level across sessions
- Destructible environment
- Weapon reload animations (reload is instant with a counter)

---

## Affected Areas

- `src/core/Npc.hpp/.cpp` — add `health`, `NpcState` enum (Idle / Fleeing / Hostile), `isArmed` flag, damage intake, flee vector, LLM combat trigger
- `src/core/Persona.hpp` — add `armed` bool field so `.persona` files can declare cops/guards as armed
- `src/core/PersonaLoader.cpp` — parse `armed = true/false` from persona files
- `src/core/World.hpp/.cpp` — add `Player` struct (health, weapon, ammo), `updateCombat(dt)`, melee/ranged hit detection, NPC->player fire logic
- `src/app/main.cpp` — left-click attack input, HUD rendering, weapon visual draw call
- `src/app/Renderer3D.hpp/.cpp` — `drawWeaponOverlay(weapon, animFrame)` for first-person arm/gun, `drawNpcAnimated(NpcVisual, state, animFrame)` for flee/recoil
- New: `src/core/Weapon.hpp` — `WeaponKind` enum, `WeaponDef` struct (damage, range, ammo capacity, fire rate, accuracy)
- New: `src/core/Player.hpp` — `Player` struct (health, `WeaponKind`, ammo map, attack cooldown, animFrame)
- New: `src/core/CombatEvents.hpp` — lightweight event structs (`MeleeHitEvent`, `ShotFiredEvent`, `NpcDamagedEvent`) passed from `World::updateCombat` to `main.cpp` to trigger LLM messages

---

## Implementation Order

1. **`Weapon.hpp` + `Player.hpp`** — define `WeaponKind` enum (`Fist`, `Pistol`), `WeaponDef` table, `Player` struct with health/ammo/cooldown. No game logic yet; just data.

2. **Add player state to `World`** — move player position out of `main.cpp` camera into `World` so combat logic can access it. `World` owns a `Player`; `main.cpp` syncs camera position from `world.player().position`.

3. **NPC health + state machine in `Npc`** — add `hp_`, `NpcState state_` (`Idle`/`Fleeing`/`Hostile`), `takeDamage(int)` method. Fleeing NPCs move away from player at fixed speed each frame; hostile (armed) NPCs move toward preferred range and fire.

4. **`CombatEvents.hpp` event structs** — simple POD structs returned from `World::updateCombat`. No allocations, no virtual dispatch.

5. **`World::updateCombat(dt)`** — melee range check on left-click, bullet travel (simple projectile list, not raycasting), NPC retaliatory fire with hit-chance roll, propagate `NpcDamagedEvent` / `ShotFiredEvent`.

6. **Attack input in `main.cpp`** — left mouse button fires `world.playerAttack()`, consuming cooldown and ammo. Dispatched combat events are checked here to trigger LLM reaction messages via `npc.ask(combatPrompt)`.

7. **LLM combat trigger** — when an `NpcDamagedEvent` arrives for an NPC or a `ShotFiredEvent` lands within hearing range of an armed NPC, build a one-shot system-injected user message: `"[GAME EVENT] You've just been attacked. Respond in character, briefly."` and call `npc.ask()`. The reply routes through the existing `pendingRoutes` map and surfaces in a small on-screen callout (not the full dialogue panel).

8. **HUD overlay in `main.cpp`** — bottom-left: red health bar + HP number. Bottom-right: weapon name + ammo `12/30`. Drawn in the SFML overlay pass with the existing `drawCenteredHudText` style.

None — plan is complete.

State Machine Design in C++ Game Entities

Lesson 0002  ·  C++17 game AI NPC  ·  Covers: src/core/Npc.hpp, src/core/Npc.cpp

The Core Idea

Every NPC in this game is always in exactly one of four states: Idle, Fleeing, Hostile, or Dead. Behaviour changes — but the state machine controls which behaviour runs.

A state machine beats a pile of boolean flags ("isAngry", "isRunning", "isDead") because:

  • States are mutually exclusive — you can't be Fleeing and Hostile at the same time
  • Transitions are explicit — the code says exactly when and why state changes
  • New behaviour is additive — adding Stunned later doesn't break Fleeing

The Code in this Game

// src/core/Npc.hpp
enum class NpcState {
    Idle,     // standing at spawn point, willing to chat
    Fleeing,  // moving away from the player at flee speed
    Hostile,  // armed NPC: moving to preferred range and firing
    Dead,     // hp reached 0; no further interaction
};

The transitions live entirely in Npc::takeDamage():

// src/core/Npc.cpp
void Npc::takeDamage(int amount) {
    if (state_ == NpcState::Dead) return;   // dead-state no-op

    hp_ -= amount;
    if (hp_ <= 0) {
        hp_ = 0;
        state_ = NpcState::Dead;            // death overrides everything
        return;
    }
    state_ = persona_.armed ? NpcState::Hostile   // armed → fight back
                            : NpcState::Fleeing;  // unarmed → run
}

Why if/else Guards Over a Switch Table?

The issue description offers two approaches:

if/else guards (used here) switch table (alternative)
One function, reads top-to-bottom like a decision tree Separate handler per state — cleaner for complex states
Cross-state logic ("hp == 0 → Dead always") is easy Must call goToDead() from each handler
Good when most transitions share logic Good when each state needs its own large behaviour block

For takeDamage, if/else wins: all three live states share the same "reduce HP, check for death" logic.

The Dead-State No-Op Pattern

Why is the first line if (state_ == NpcState::Dead) return;?

Because combat events can arrive in bursts. Two bullets might hit the same NPC on the same frame. Without the guard, the second call would subtract more HP from 0, push HP negative, and re-set state to Hostile or Fleeing — resurrecting a dead NPC. The guard is a defensive boundary: once Dead, forever Dead.

Where the State Is Used

The state machine drives both AI and rendering:

  • World::tickNpcAi() — the switch on combatState() picks the movement code
  • Renderer3D::drawNpc() — could collapse the figure visually for Dead NPCs (future work)
  • main.cpp — skips LLM combat triggers for Dead NPCs
// World::tickNpcAi() — the state drives the per-frame behaviour
switch (npc.combatState()) {
    case NpcState::Fleeing:
        // move away from player via city_.resolveMovement
        break;
    case NpcState::Hostile:
        // advance/back-off to preferred range, fire on cooldown
        break;
    default:  // Idle, Dead — no movement
        break;
}

Extending the State Machine

To add a Stunned state:

  1. Add Stunned to the enum
  2. Add a case NpcState::Stunned: break; in tickNpcAi() (no movement)
  3. Add a transition — e.g. "grenade hit → Stunned for 2 s → prior state"

Existing Flee/Hostile code is untouched.

Key takeaway: State machines make "impossible" game states impossible by construction. The NPC can't be Hostile and Dead — the enum has only one value at a time. No boolean-flag combination can accidentally set both.

Probabilistic Game AI: Dice Rolls and Preferred-Range Enemies

Lesson 0003  ·  C++17 game AI combat  ·  Covers: src/core/World.cpp — tickNpcAi()

The Problem with Deterministic AI

If a cop always hit the player, combat would be frustrating; always missed, pointless. The sweet spot is probabilistic accuracy: the player feels at risk but not helpless. Simple dice rolls create interesting gameplay that deterministic formulas can't match.

The Accuracy Roll

The cop fires a "virtual bullet" each cooldown cycle. Whether it lands is a single uniform random number between 0 and 1, compared against kNpcHitChance: 

// src/core/World.cpp — tickNpcAi()
const bool landed =
    std::uniform_real_distribution<float>(0.f, 1.f)(rng_) < kNpcHitChance;

With kNpcHitChance = 0.70f, the cop hits 70% of the time on average. The rng_ is a std::mt19937 seeded once in the World constructor — no new RNG object created per shot.

Why std::mt19937?

Mersenne Twister has a very long period (219937−1) and passes statistical tests. std::rand() is unreliable and slow. mt19937 is the C++11 standard answer for game RNG.

Fire Cooldown Variance

Shots arrive at random intervals between 1.2 s and 2.0 s: 

npc.fireCooldown = kNpcFireCooldownMin +
    std::uniform_real_distribution<float>(
        0.f, kNpcFireCooldownMax - kNpcFireCooldownMin)(rng_);
// = 1.2 + uniform(0, 0.8) → somewhere in [1.2, 2.0]

Randomising cooldowns prevents the "metronome effect" — a cop that fires at exactly 1.5 s is predictable and easy to dodge. Variance makes the fight feel more natural.

Preferred-Range Movement

Armed NPCs don't just stand still and shoot. They try to stay at a "sweet spot" distance from the player — close enough to threaten, far enough to avoid melee:

Player Cop o ←————— 8 units ———————→ 👮 | < 7 units | 7–9 units | > 9 units | | cop backs | cop stays | cop chases | | off | and fires | player |
const float dist = distanceXZ(npc.position(), player_.position);
const Vec3 dir   = normalize(player_.position - npc.position());

if (dist > kHostilePreferRange + 1.f) {
    // Too far — advance
    const Vec3 target = npc.position() + dir * (kFleeSpeed * dt);
    npc.position() = city_.resolveMovement(npc.position(), target, 0.4f);
} else if (dist < kHostilePreferRange - 1.f) {
    // Too close — back off
    const Vec3 target = npc.position() - dir * (kFleeSpeed * dt);
    npc.position() = city_.resolveMovement(npc.position(), target, 0.4f);
}
// In the 1-unit dead-zone around 8: no movement, just fire

The ±1 unit dead-zone around kHostilePreferRange stops the NPC jittering when the player is right at the boundary.

Why city_.resolveMovement() Instead of Direct Assignment?

The city is full of buildings. If the cop moved by directly adding to position, they'd walk through walls. City::resolveMovement(from, to, radius) does AABB sliding — the same collision code the player uses. An NPC that respects walls feels real; one that phases through them breaks immersion.

Circle Collision for Projectiles

Player bullets also need to hit NPCs. The v1 simplification: each NPC is a vertical cylinder — radius 0.4, height 1.8. A bullet hits if:

  1. XZ distance from bullet to NPC centre < 0.4 (inside the circle)
  2. Bullet Y position is in [0, 1.8] (inside the height)
const float xzDist = distanceXZ(proj.position, npc.position());
if (xzDist > kNpcRadius) continue;                        // outside circle
if (proj.position.y < 0.f || proj.position.y > kNpcHeight) continue; // above/below
// hit!

No mesh collision, no raycasting — just two number comparisons. Fast enough to check every projectile against every NPC every frame.

Design insight: Simple dice rolls produce more interesting gameplay than deterministic damage because they create tension. A 70% hit chance means the player can get unlucky (three hits in a row) or lucky (two misses). That variance — not the average — is what makes fights memorable.

LLM as Reactive Game Component

Lesson 0004  ·  LLM async game architecture  ·  Covers: src/app/main.cpp — combat reaction system

The Core Pattern

An LLM reply takes hundreds of milliseconds — a game can't block waiting for it. The solution: fire-and-forget.
